# Applications: Where basketball analytics goes next (SSAC22 panel)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Keep Applied Performance output flowing through staff, not to athletes directly. The panel's rule was that analysts brief coaches, trainers or physicians, who carry it to players, and that the analyst starts from the staff member's question [19:19]. For football this means a weekly monitoring flag goes to Athletic Performance or Athletic Medicine with a stated question it answers.
- Inference: Use limb-side asymmetry as a return-to-play flag. The panel described landing asymmetry after an ACL tear and secondary tendon and back complaints [12:42]. A concrete Baylor version: report left-right difference from single-leg jump testing for athletes in lower-body return-to-play, and ask Athletic Medicine whether the side gap is the question they have.
- Inference: Frame every monitoring alert as a decision, not a prediction. One panelist argued that knowing the predicted outcome is useless to a team unless it points at what to change [45:53]. Each flag in a report should name the action it would change.
- Inference: Judge a staff member's or a program's analytics contribution over a long window, not game to game, since a panelist said a one-game read is a tiny sample [35:10].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supplies information that supports Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine decisions, in a support role (Explicit, Playbook). The panel's conduit idea agrees closely.
- Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for the roster after about a year because athletes learned to game them, but kept in return-to-play and chronic-condition cases (Explicit). The panel gives a different reason for athlete distrust of monitoring (employer use of health data, contracts) [14:44]; it does not discuss gaming. Extends, not conflicts.
- Eric's baseline: injury risk can be reduced but not eliminated, and no formal injury-risk model is attributed to him (Inferred, course material). A panelist said he is not building models to predict catastrophic injuries [19:50] and another said you cannot hand analysts injury data and ask who tears an ACL next month [19:50]. Agrees.
- Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye matters as much as technology (Inferred, course team position, speaker unconfirmed). Bob's point that what a coach sees is already data [22:54] agrees. That also sits in tension with Eric's own replacement of surveys by objective force-plate readings; the panel does not resolve it.

## What would have to be true

- Staff must have a question first. Without a named requester in Athletic Medicine or Athletic Performance, a flag has nowhere to go.
- Side-to-side asymmetry needs a reference: the athlete's own pre-injury or prior-season values, and a repeatable test protocol, before any gap is called meaningful.
- Any data used for return-to-play or injury discussion has to be handled as health information. Catherine Evans raised this as a compliance issue [18:18]; check with Athletic Medicine what rules cover our records.

## Do not apply when

- The claim at issue is basketball-specific or NBA-specific. The no-wearables rule, contract incentives and star-player load-management politics [13:43] [21:53] do not map to a college football roster.
- Someone treats the ACL examples as evidence. They are two named cases and one coach's view about one-legged moves [11:41]; no rates were given.
- Someone wants to cite "we've maxed out the data" [22:23] as a reason to stop collecting. It is one panelist's opinion about basketball, in an opposite direction to what is actually unfinished in football data (see sport-specific thresholds).
- The athlete's own trainer or private data is involved. The panel noted such numbers may never reach the team [47:23]; do not assume access.

## First step

Pick one athlete currently in lower-body return-to-play, pull the existing left-right difference from his single-leg jump trials, and ask Athletic Medicine one question: is this the number they want, or something else.

# Applications: The reformation of the NCAA (SSAC22 panel)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Add outside commitments to the athlete context. A panelist said NIL involves real work (building audiences, marketing, dealing with lawyers and accountants) on top of a full-time student and athlete job [41:02]. Ask Athletic Performance and the position coaches whether time demands from NIL should be a standing item in weekly monitoring conversations, next to class and travel.
- Inference: Treat transfer and recruiting grades as one input among several now that NIL may influence where players go. The moderator said NIL likely played a role in where recruits chose and that the NCAA planned to review transfers for NIL involvement [02:06] [12:19]. A specific use: keep a log of incoming transfers with the PFF-based grade at arrival and what they did in the first season, so the grading approach is checked against results rather than reputation.
- Inference: Prepare for data-governance questions if athletes are ever classified as employees. Panelists named unresolved issues (Title IX application, taxation of income and scholarship, overtime, collective bargaining) [31:46] [38:00]. For monitoring data (GPS, force plate), that suggests writing down now who owns the data, who sees it, and how long it is kept.
- Inference: Track travel as a load factor for non-football sports if realignment adds distance. The talk gave a softball travel anecdote [45:37] and said geography is driven by football television value [46:08].

## Eric's baseline

No direct link found.

## What would have to be true

- The relevant rule set must be confirmed at Baylor by compliance (state law, NCAA interim policy, the conference). The panel described a state-by-state patchwork as of March 2022 [05:09]; it may have changed.
- For a transfer log, enough incoming transfers over several seasons to compare grade and outcome; one class is too few.
- For any data-governance step, legal and compliance owners decide, not Applied Performance.

## Do not apply when

- Deciding something about Baylor or the Big 12: no panelist spoke for them, and the Big East commissioner's league is basketball-centric [43:05].
- Using numbers from the panel as current. They are from March 2022 (for example the guess that most NIL deals are under 2 to 3 thousand dollars, which the speaker said depends on the data set and that she hesitated to confirm [13:22]).
- Reading the employee-status discussion as a prediction. Panelists called it possible, not likely [39:31], and the cases cited were filings and a pending appeals-court case, not outcomes [36:28].
- Valuing athletes by social reach: the Wasserman speaker said an athlete's following is often alumni, not students [16:25], and that is one agency's view of audience, not a performance measure.

## First step

Ask compliance for the current one-page summary of what the department may and may not do regarding NIL and transfer conversations, and save it with the date next to the recruiting grading notes.

---
type: video-summary
video_id: 4dTGHEHQLwM
title: "SSAC22: The Reformation of the NCAA: The Impact of New Legislation, Re-Alignment, and NIL"
event: SSAC22 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Val Ackerman, Elizabeth Lindsay, Amy Privett Perko (caption spelling "amy prevet perco"), Michelle Steele (moderator), Emily Bridges (host)]
topics: [policy, competitive-advantage, other-sport:college-athletics-governance]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A four-woman panel reviews where college athletics stood in March 2022: roughly nine months into name, image and likeness (NIL) with no national rule, a patchwork of state laws, and weak NCAA enforcement. They discuss how an agency values athletes, whether athletes could become employees through labor-board charges, proposals to split fifty-bowl-subdivision football governance from the rest of the NCAA, conference realignment after Texas and Oklahoma moved, and what NIL means for women's sports. Each speaker represents an institution (a conference, a reform commission, a sports agency), so views reflect those positions. It matters for anyone whose athletes, recruits or transfers are affected by these rules.

## Key claims

- Pre-pandemic college sports revenue was about 18.9 billion dollars, mostly from Division I basketball and football (moderator's figure) [01:05].
- Without a national NIL standard the result is what was expected: a mix of state laws, and loose NCAA parameters where a state has no law [04:08] [05:09].
- Attempts at a national rule failed over legal concerns, and the appeal to Congress to override the states did not work either [05:09].
- The Supreme Court decision (caption spelling "austin") undercut the NCAA's confidence in its rule-making authority, which made it hesitant to write a framework open to legal challenge [10:17] [10:47].
- The NCAA's stated policy bars NIL as a recruiting inducement but is not enforced; the speaker compared this to pro sports, where salary caps limit such offers [07:42] [08:13].
- Congress is unlikely to act soon (election year, other priorities), and the panel said nothing "utterly chaotic" had happened yet: a patchwork but not a mess [11:17] [11:47].
- One speaker said the middle of the NIL deal distribution is small, with typical deals well below the headline figures; she hedged on the exact median pending full data [13:22].
- The agency values athletes using two data types: audience analytics and performance measurement [15:23].
- Brands often misjudge the audience: a college athlete's social following is mostly alumni and other fans of the school, not fellow students [16:25].
- The Big East has no conference NIL policy because its schools sit in different jurisdictions with differing laws [18:58].
- An NCAA working group had proposed a third-party administrator and disclosure so deals could be tracked and fair market value distinguished from recruiting inducements [19:58] [20:29].
- The NCAA does not bar schools from helping arrange NIL deals, which raises institutional involvement and Title IX questions (for example staffing for football versus Olympic sports) [21:30] [22:01].
- The Knight Commission speaker framed a choice between co-curricular sport and commercial venture, with some schools likely to pick each [22:32].
- Women athletes were described as well placed for NIL because they have had to build an off-field voice, and evidence of NIL activity extends to volleyball, soccer, swimming and women's basketball [24:34] [25:37] [26:07].
- Labor-board charges against USC, UCLA and the Pac-12 seek employee status for athletes; a September general-counsel memo opened that door [03:06] [30:46].
- Employee classification would raise open issues: Title IX, taxability of income and scholarships, overtime, termination, unionization; the speaker doubted anyone had thought these through [31:46] [38:00] [38:30].
- The Knight Commission proposes a separate body to govern football, joining revenue and rules authority and putting football athletes on the board; and a new Division I financial framework tying shared revenues to education, health and safety [33:21] [33:51] [34:55].
- Its data claim: new revenue over about 15 years flowed disproportionately to salaries and facilities [35:26].
- The 2010 realignment brought about two billion dollars in new revenue to major conferences; one speaker said football-driven alignment produces illogical travel for other sports [45:06] [45:37].
- Conference exit is mainly a notice period plus an exit fee, negotiated; the speaker expected contracts to be honored [48:11].
- The board's intent was "no harm" to Divisions II and III, and the men's basketball tournament holds Division I together [52:16] [52:47].
- A survey of college students, run for five years, finds students value an athlete's off-field voice as much as on-field performance [54:21].
- Market size matters for NIL; a bigger stage means more audience [55:25].

## Numbers and definitions

- 18.9 billion dollars revenue, year before the pandemic [01:05]. Later a speaker says "18 billion" with at least 3 billion going back as scholarships; the captions are garbled near "college boards" [28:42].
- 50,000 dollars to a Texas offensive lineman, described as for charitable purposes [12:19].
- "Under 2 3k" deal sizes for the middle of the market (garbled; likely 2 to 3 thousand dollars, speaker hedged) [13:22].
- About 500,000 college athletes, speaker's figure [28:12].
- About 6,000 dollars per student cash award said to be possible after the court decision [29:45].
- College football playoff: 500 million dollars annually, 1.5 billion if expanded to 12 teams; the NCAA makes zero revenue from FBS football [33:21] [33:51].
- Shared athletic revenue: more than 3 billion annually [34:55].
- Big East: 11 jurisdictions, 8 in states with an NIL law [18:58].
- 351 schools in Division I [52:47].
- 700,000 Instagram followers for a UConn player before college (speaker's figure, caption garbled "i think a") [54:21].
- 4 percent of media coverage for women's sports (speaker's figure) [55:25].
- "Nine schools" trying to leave Conference USA; three not following exit provisions [46:39] [47:09].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Agency valuation: audience analytics (front end) plus performance measurement (back end) [15:23].
- Knight Commission proposals for football governance and financial framework; a Knight-Newhouse college athletics database is named [34:55] [35:26].

## Summary

Five people look ahead from the 2012 research era of basketball analytics. Most of the first half is about biomechanics: data moving "inside the athlete's body", why current tracking only gives center-of-mass dots, and how to use movement data for skill and injury work. The sharper thread is trust. Panelists say analytics groups have often failed to build it with players, that health data raises privacy and compliance duties, and that the useful role is a conduit who answers staff questions rather than approaching players. Later topics: whether data is "maxed out", draft prediction, chemistry, causal inference, and shooting variance. Many points are panelists' opinions or anecdotes; no data are shown.

## Key claims

- The panel started from 2012 papers on skill-based chemistry, optical-tracking rebounds and spatial shooting analysis [01:32] [02:02].
- Kirk Goldsberry says the next frontier is biomechanics: the data are moving inside athletes' bodies, modeled on baseball pitching labs [02:33] [03:03].
- Each person has a unique movement strategy, so prescribing one way to shoot is wrong; the goal is to explain why a given athlete succeeds [04:04] [05:04].
- Measuring outcomes is advanced, but how a coaching change causes a better shot is not, and whether the fix repeats or transfers is open [05:35].
- Allison Feaster says players hear too many voices; analysts should equip coaches with the language and go to the head coach, not to a player [06:05] [06:36] [07:37].
- Bob Voulgaris says league tracking gives only center-of-mass blobs, so real biomechanics needs a lab with a marker suit, which is unpleasant but the only route to accurate joint centers now [08:39] [09:10] [09:40].
- Goldsberry expects computer vision to remove markers within about five years [09:40].
- Biomechanics might first flag injury risk (for example knee valgus on a Euro step, and landing asymmetry after an ACL tear) [11:41] [12:11] [12:42].
- A panelist cites a coach's view that more one-legged moves explain injuries [11:41].
- Bob says the players' association rules bar wearables during games; the risk is health data hurting contracts [13:43].
- Players are skeptical of employer collection of health data; one panelist said the analytics community has a trust problem [14:14] [14:44] [16:16].
- Goldsberry says analytics groups have more often botched than succeeded at the conduit role and need athlete buy-in, shifting from surveillance to empowerment [17:17] [17:47].
- Catherine Evans says health data at scale becomes protected health information with HIPAA-like duties, so she works through trainers and physicians who bring specific questions [18:18] [19:19].
- Predicting an ACL tear from a pile of injury data is not realistic (Evans); Goldsberry says he is not building catastrophic-injury prediction [19:50].
- Pulling a star for rest based on sports-science data creates coach-player tension, and Feaster has no ready answer; she notes star adoption of load management is uneven [20:51] [21:23] [21:53].
- Bob says tracking data and data generally are "maxed out", that a coach seeing fatigue is itself data, and that more data will not change much for elite players [22:23] [22:54] [23:25].
- Baseball is ahead partly because it is easier to analyze (closed tasks) and its smallest analytics group is larger than basketball's largest; football is expected to catch up thanks to public data [27:32] [28:03] [29:04].
- Measuring mindset: panelists do not know the brain domain, doubt players would accept it, and cite a psychologist question on traffic lights and the Celtics' earlier brain-type scouting as odd examples [30:36] [31:06] [32:39].
- A midseason surge is explained by long-season factors (new leadership, staff, switching defense gelling, an Olympics hangover); a panelist said judging analytics game by game is a small-sample mistake [34:10] [34:40] [35:10].
- The draft is hard because players are younger, experiences vary, and nobody knows what the league looks like years out [35:40] [36:10] [37:10].
- In ten years the panel expects variations on today's themes: reproducibility, shooting, and rules-of-thumb that shift as the league changes, such as post-ups and the debate on threes [38:41] [39:41] [40:11].
- Goldsberry wants the future to bring analytics to athlete development and wellness, with sleep science as a non-invasive example [41:43] [42:15].
- Feaster would like to measure how people mesh in a coaching staff or organization; Evans says chemistry measures would need data at scale [42:48] [44:21].
- Evans says teams only care about prediction as far as it tells them what to change, and wants causal inference papers [45:23] [45:53] [46:23].
- Goldsberry notes athletes and private trainers (Curry and his shooting coach is the example) use numbers teams never see [46:53] [47:23].
- Shot changes are possible (examples given are Kawhi Leonard and Tony Parker), and consistency of movement pattern is what to diagnose [48:55] [49:25].
- Bob says gamblers learn to live with game-to-game variance; the expected shot-quality metric from a tracking vendor helped show coaches a loss was luck [50:56] [51:57] [52:58].
- For slumps, one approach is to update a prior using gym numbers and past season rather than panic [55:00] [55:30].

## Numbers and definitions

- Camera tracking started in 2010, full-league adoption in 2013 (Bob; caption "2010 i think") [08:39].
- 2012 papers named: three, plus Goldsberry's spatial shooting paper [01:32] [02:02].
- Heart-rate variability "gone up by 6.7" is a hypothetical example, not data [22:54].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Optical tracking data (center of mass only) [08:39].

## Limits and open questions

## Summary

A Catapult product manager demonstrates a product that places wearable physical data (sprints, impacts, heart rate, player load) inside a video and event-data platform, MatchTracker, after Catapult and its maker joined last year. He argues three benefits: context for physical numbers by syncing them to video and game state, profiling the physical demands of a style of play to design practice, and saving analyst time. Examples come from one MLS match, rugby scrums and a football tempo scenario. It is a vendor demo, so claims of benefit are commercial and not independently tested. Live use and several sports are on the roadmap, not available.

## Key claims

- Video editors let teams tag events and sync them to video, which was the start of modern analysis in soccer [00:30] [01:00].
- Positional data came separately, and the problem is data produced by different providers and analyzed in different software [02:01] [02:31].
- SBG Sports released MatchTracker in 2015 to integrate event data, video and positional data [03:01].
- Physical data come from wearables and are used for injury risk, return to play and load across a season [04:04] [04:35].
- Catapult joined SBG last year to bring physical data into MatchTracker [04:35] [05:05].
- A total like 15 sprints or 6 miles is not enough for coaching; the coach wants to know why the player was running [05:35] [06:05].
- Syncing each sprint to video lets a coach click any sprint, see the run, and share a clip with the team [06:35] [07:06].
- Impacts can be graphed by 5-minute block and sorted by force, with video behind each [07:36] [08:07].
- Physical data can be broken down by game state, such as offense versus defense, phase of play or how a sequence ended [08:38] [09:08].
- In rugby, wearables detect scrums by machine learning, giving who was involved, time to get back up, and effect on heart rate and load [09:38] [10:09].
- Physical data can quantify the toll of a style of play, such as high pressing; measuring every press in a season gives a profile of physical requirements [11:41] [12:11] [13:42].
- Because athletes wear the same device in practice, one can compare practice to game and see who practices at game speed [13:42] [14:13].
- A football tempo offense can be measured by speed, accelerations, decelerations and load per play or drive, to see who meets the requirements and for training and injury prevention [14:13] [14:44].
